items.title: US publishers file lawsuit against Google for 'training Gemini on copyrighted books'
items.excerpt: Hachette, Cengage, Elsevier and author Scott Turow filed a new US class action against Google, alleging it illegally copied millions of copyrighted works from Google Books, Play and Scholar to train its Gemini AI models. It is the first major AI-training suit to target Google beyond the Anthropic/Bloomsbury frame.

items.title: New York Times journalist investigates origins of AI-generated nonfiction
items.excerpt: When NYT journalist Kashmir Hill found an AI-generated biography of herself for sale on Amazon, she bought and read it, then tried to trace its author, exposing how machine-written nonfiction is quietly filling retail catalogs. A pointed look at AI-authored books and the collapse of authorship signals for readers.

items.title: Researchers to investigate local editor and publisher AI use
items.excerpt: University of Melbourne researchers Katherine Day and Sharon Mullins and RMIT's Rose Michael have launched a survey of Australian publishers and editors about how they use generative AI tools in day-to-day editorial work. The study aims to map real adoption in editing, production and workflow across the local industry.

items.title: Guest Post — Research Needs a Shared Standard for AI Disclosure
items.excerpt: Drawing on the World Conferences on Research Integrity, this piece argues scholarly publishing needs standardized frameworks for disclosing AI use, as authors and reviewers remain confused about what transparency requirements actually apply. A push to make AI-disclosure a consistent part of the publishing workflow.

items.title: Some Listeners Prefer AI Narration for Multi-Voice Audiobooks
items.excerpt: In a survey by AI audiobook company Spoken, 61% of fiction listeners mistook some AI narration for a human voice, and 65% said they were likely to listen to a full multi-cast AI audiobook after hearing a sample, up from 31% beforehand. The findings point to growing acceptance of AI multi-voice narration even as blanket interest in AI voices wanes.

items.title: Open Science 2.0: Building Understanding in an AI-Mediated World
items.excerpt: As AI assistants increasingly mediate how research is discovered and read, this essay argues open science must shift focus from mere access to trust, interpretation and effective communication. It reframes what publishers and libraries owe readers when a machine, not a person, is doing the reading.

items.title: The Tools Book Banners Are Using to Target Books in 2026
items.excerpt: A look at the software now shaping which books get flagged, including BookLens, an AI-powered book-rating tool that 'hallucinates' and fabricates content details for titles that sometimes don't even exist. A cautionary case study in how unreliable generative-AI book analysis is being wired into discovery, rating and gatekeeping decisions across schools and libraries.
